pending_items.title: EU-Indonesia trade deal opens new markets, but challenges remain
pending_items.content:
As the European Union seeks to deepen its presence in Asia and diversify its trade relationships, Indonesia is emerging as an increasingly important partner.

At a signing ceremony in Brussels last week , European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the bloc's trade agreement with Jakarta as one of its "most ambitious deals" in the region, linking markets of 730 million people.

The deal, the culmination of nearly a decade of negotiations, reflects the EU's efforts to diversify its trade partnerships, secure access to critical raw materials and reduce strategic dependencies on China .

For Indonesia, it offers opportunities to attract investment, expand exports and strengthen its position in global supply chains.

The agreement will gradually scrap tariffs on more than 98% of product categories, covering almost the entire value of bilateral trade over 15 years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For the EU, gaining better access to critical raw materials, particularly nickel, and diversifying its supply chains are central to its strategic partnership with Indonesia, said Philip Schleifer, an associate professor of political science at the University of Amsterdam.

"The main strategic interests are opening up a large and growing market for European companies, diversifying and deepening its economic partnerships, reducing strategic dependencies on China, and securing access to critical raw materials," Schleifer told DW.

Indonesia's mineral resources are particularly important for Europe's green and digital transitions. Nickel, for instance, is a key material for batteries and electric vehicles.

The agreement also creates opportunities for European investment in strategic sectors, including electric vehicles, electronics and pharmaceuticals.

But Indonesia has its own industrial ambitions. The government wants to move beyond exporting raw materials by developing domestic processing industries and retaining more value from its natural resources.

"The challenge for the EU is to reconcile its own interest in securing raw material supply with Indonesia's industrial development objectives," said Eline Blot, a senior policy analyst at the Institute for European Environmental Policy (IEEP).

For Jakarta, the agreement offers opportunities to expand exports, attract investment and strengthen its position in global supply chains.

Yose Rizal Damuri, an economist at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said his institution's study estimates Indonesian exports could increase by around 60% in the coming years.

"Not only can Indonesia increase exports to Europe, but it can also become more strongly integrated into the global supply chains of European companies," Yose told DW.

Potential beneficiaries include labor-intensive manufacturing sectors such as textiles, garments, footwear and furniture, alongside other Indonesian commodities and manufactured products.

The agreement could also encourage European investment and create employment opportunities. However, Yose stressed that access to the European market does not automatically translate into higher exports.

He identified three priorities for Indonesia: raising awareness of the agreement among domestic businesses, strengthening production capacity and improving the country's business climate.

"Various trade agreements signed by Indonesia have relatively low utilization rates. The value of exports using these facilities remains limited compared with overall export values," he said, emphasizing the need for better information and outreach to producers.

Syafruddin Karimi, an economist at Andalas University, also highlighted the opportunity to diversify Indonesia's export markets and reduce dependence on major trading partners such as China, the United States and regional Asian economies.

However, he warned that Indonesian producers must improve their compliance with European standards .

"Products must be traceable, including whether their production involves environmental damage or labor practices that undermine human dignity," Karimi said.

He added that smaller businesses would need greater government support to meet requirements concerning raw materials, production processes and workers' rights.

The expansion of trade and investment could also increase environmental pressures, particularly in nickel mining, palm oil production and manufacturing.

IEEP analyst Blot warned that increased production without stronger environmental safeguards could worsen pollution, ecosystem degradation and industrial emissions. " Nickel mining and processing can contribute to pollution and ecosystem degradation , while palm oil remains closely associated with deforestation," she said.

The growing importance of Indonesian iron and steel exports also raises concerns about emissions from energy-intensive production.

The EU's Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) presents another challenge for Indonesian producers, particularly small-scale farmers who may lack the resources, technical capacity and documentation needed to demonstrate compliance.

Blot acknowledged that these requirements could create disproportionate costs for smaller producers and potentially favor larger companies.

However, she cautioned against using smallholders' livelihoods as an argument to weaken environmental regulations.

Some Indonesian smallholder organisations, she noted, have supported the EUDR as an opportunity to improve accountability in the palm oil industry.

"Rather than weakening environmental requirements, the priority should be to ensure that smallholders receive adequate financial and technical support to meet them," she said.

Professor Schleifer at the University of Amsterdam also warned that growing global demand for Indonesian natural resources could create environmental and social problems previously associated with commodities such as timber, palm oil and coal.

While Indonesia has considerable bargaining power because of its mineral wealth, the challenge is ensuring that increased demand translates into domestic industrial development rather than simply expanding resource extraction.

The agreement includes a dedicated Trade and Sustainable Development chapter covering climate change, biodiversity conservation, sustainable forest management and labor rights. It also provides mechanisms for cooperation and civil society participation.

However, there is no guarantee these commitments will be implemented. "Experience with other EU trade agreements suggests that there is often a big gap between sustainability commitments on paper and outcomes on the ground," Schleifer said.

Blot similarly called for a time-bound roadmap with measurable objectives, stronger monitoring and meaningful participation from civil society and local communities.

For Indonesia, the challenge also lies in preparing domestic industries to compete. Karimi stressed that the government, both at national and regional levels, must work with businesses to improve production standards, particularly among small and medium-sized enterprises.

Yose also emphasized the importance of a predictable business environment, warning that frequent policy changes and regulatory uncertainty could discourage investors.

"Without improvements in the domestic business climate, this will not become a reality. Everything will remain good on paper but will not turn into real momentum for change," he said.

Ultimately, the trade agreement offers Indonesia an opportunity to strengthen its position in international trade and attract investment from Europe.

But whether the agreement delivers broader economic benefits will depend on the country's ability to develop competitive industries , move into higher-value production, and ensure that environmental protection and workers' rights are not overlooked.

DW's Muhammad Athif Aiman contributed to this article.

pending_items.title: Haftar meets Erdogan: Can Turkiye reunify Libya as it courts rival sides?
pending_items.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan hosted eastern Libyan military commander Khalifa Haftar in Ankara on Wednesday, days after the Tripoli-based prime minister from the rival administration held talks with the Turkish foreign minister in Istanbul.

Haftar’s first trip to Ankara comes nearly seven years after Turkiye helped the internationally recognised Government of National Accord (GNA) repel a military offensive led by his self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA).

But following the 2020 United Nations-brokered ceasefire, Turkiye has pivoted towards a pragmatic approach, working to bring the rival administrations towards a unified government and military as it seeks to safeguard its maritime interests in the Mediterranean Sea.

The meetings come ahead of an expected visit by Erdogan to Libya, his first in 15 years, as Ankara seeks to reconcile the country’s rival administrations.

So what are Ankara’s interests in forging closer ties with Haftar, and what are the challenges ahead as Ankara seeks to reunify Libya?

Turkiye’s 2019-20 military intervention in support of the Tripoli-based government turned the tide of the Libyan civil war, forcing Khalifa Haftar’s forces to retreat from western Libya. But after the ceasefire later that year, Ankara began establishing contacts with the eastern authorities.

This rapprochement accelerated in 2025, after the United States launched efforts to reconcile Libya’s rival governments. A concurrent UN track produced the 4+4 agreement this past August, a political roadmap for a unified government and nationwide presidential and parliamentary elections within two years.

Turkiye was among the states to welcome and encourage the reconciliation process, while deepening its diplomatic and military ties with the east. In July, Ankara reached agreements with Haftar’s LNA on military infrastructure and training.

Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya analyst, told Al Jazeera that Turkiye’s military strength and staying power have granted it prestige across Libya.

“Today, no Libyan leader of consequence can afford to spurn Ankara,” he said.

Of particular importance to Ankara’s relations with Libya is a maritime boundary agreement that it signed with the Tripoli-based government in 2019, but which was only adopted by the east last month.

The deal is a political flashpoint for several countries in the Eastern Mediterranean, opposed by Greece and Israel, and has been criticised by Egypt, which argued that it violated its own maritime rights.

But Ankara has defended the agreement as lawful.

Turkiye has sought to bring Libya’s rival military leaderships together. In May, Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler met Abdulsalam al-Zoubi, the deputy defence minister in Tripoli, and Saddam Haftar, Khalifa Haftar’s son and a senior LNA commander. Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin later met Saddam Haftar in the eastern city of Benghazi.

In October, Ankara hosted further talks on military reunification, including discussions on establishing a joint military command in the central city of Sirte. However, disagreements over who would exercise political authority over a unified military remain unresolved.

On the economic front, Turkiye was among 10 countries that welcomed Libya’s adoption of its first unified national budget in more than a decade.

Ankara has also coordinated its diplomatic efforts with other countries involved in the reconciliation process. In June, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan held talks in Cairo with his Egyptian and Saudi counterparts and with Massad Boulos, a senior adviser to US President Donald Trump.

In August, Fidan travelled to Tripoli and Benghazi for separate meetings with Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah and Khalifa Haftar respectively.

Ankara has, however, not publicly endorsed a specific power-sharing arrangement. US mediators have backed a contentious proposal to make Saddam Haftar chairman of the Presidency Council, the three-member body that serves as Libya’s head of state.

It is unclear whether Erdogan’s December visit will bring Dbeibah and Khalifa Haftar together for direct negotiations. No such meeting has been confirmed.

For Turkiye, much is at stake in Libyan reconciliation. Ankara has military and economic interests in both parts of the country, as well as the maritime boundary agreement that underpins its claims to potentially gas-rich waters in the Eastern Mediterranean.

Bringing Libya under a single government would allow Ankara to pursue its defence, energy and reconstruction agreements within a unified institutional framework.

“Turkiye has gone from backing one side to engaging both because a stable, unified Libya best protects its economic and maritime interests,” said Sansom Milton, a senior research fellow at the Center for Conflict and Humanitarian Studies.

Saban Kardas, a research professor at Qatar University, told Al Jazeera that the effort was also in line with Turkiye’s historic approach to diplomacy with a divided state.

“The idea is to push for a national unity of some form. To make engagement sustainable, you need to see some measure of national unity,” he said.

Although Ankara is currently well-positioned with Tripoli and Benghazi, analysts told Al Jazeera that instability and diverging visions of who will lead a reconciled Libya present major hurdles.

“Despite the assets and advantages Turkiye has accumulated in Libya, the country remains volatile,” Harchaoui said.

Libya is grappling with a deepening economic crisis, a weakening dinar, rising living costs, fuel and cash shortages and deteriorating public services. All of these have led to an increase in protests and strikes over the past year, casting a shadow over efforts for political stability.

While Saddam Haftar’s proposed appointment as chairman of the Presidency Council has the backing of US mediators, it faces opposition from powerful armed and political factions in western Libya, particularly in Misrata.

The city, a stronghold of the 2011 uprising that toppled Muammar Gaddafi, also helped defeat Khalifa Haftar’s offensive in 2020.

“A further difficulty is that western Libya has no single chain of command, so leaders in Tripoli cannot guarantee that the armed groups around them will accept a deal reached in their name,” said Milton, of the Center for Conflict and Humanitarian Studies.

“The main challenge is that division remains profitable for elites and armed groups on each side, who control separate revenues and institutions and have little incentive to merge them,” he added.

Kardas said, “It comes down to the local parties to put aside their differences and work through their deadlocks and divisions.”
